paragraphs: Rav Yosef son of Rav Ilai.

In [Sukkah 26a](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.26a.11-13), Rav Ashi says, “It is a decree lest he fall asleep.” Hyman comments that this is a scribal error: it should read Rava, from which the wording “Rav Ashi” arose. The Ritva likewise has Rava, while Dikdukei Soferim reads Rav Yosef. Abaye said to him, “But what of the teaching—” Rav Yosef son of Rav Ilai said: “[This refers] to someone who entrusts his sleep to others.” Rav Mesharshiya objected: “Your guarantor needs a guarantor.” Rav Mesharshiya is known to have been Rava’s disciple.[^1][^2]

notes.text: Hyman’s elliptical phrase ונעשה מהרב אשי is rendered in its immediate context: the reading he regards as correct, Rava, became “Rav Ashi.” This conveys the direction of his proposed corruption without supplying a particular mechanism or silently changing the Hebrew. The complete printed notice on volume II, p. 753 (PDF page 336), including the small-type parenthesis, was consulted. His claim about Rav Mesharshiya’s discipleship remains his own historical assertion. The bracketed words make במוסר שינתו לאחרים grammatical without adding a legal condition; the dash preserves the source’s abbreviated question.

The William Davidson vocalized Hebrew text of Sukkah 26a:11–13 retains Rav Ashi and explicitly writes Rav Yosef son of Rav Ilai and Rav Mesharshiya. The text retrieved under Sefaria’s “Ritva on Sukkah 26a” does read Rava in the matching opening quotation; its supplied version metadata is titled “Chiddushei HaRashba, Sheva Shitot, Warsaw, 1883.” That catalog/edition-label discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved here. Hyman’s Ritva attribution and the separately reported Dikdukei Soferim reading remain his attributions; the latter has not been independently checked. No version is silently substituted for Hyman’s discussion, and no identity binding is made.
